fact: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information search with a language model that writes an answer using the information found.
The 2020 RAG paper describes combining a model's stored knowledge with a separate, searchable collection of documents.
A model may not have access to a person's private documents or the latest changes unless those details are supplied to it.
Before answering, a RAG system searches its knowledge collection for information related to the user's question.
The system adds the question and selected information to the model's input; the model then writes an answer using that context.
A common preparation step splits long documents into smaller pieces, called chunks, so search can return selected parts instead of whole documents.
An embedding is a list of numbers made from text; it represents some of the text's meaning and context.
When text has a similar meaning, its embedding is often near another similar text's embedding, even when the words differ.
A vector search index stores numerical text representations and can find entries whose representations are close to a question's representation.
A vector database or index can be used to keep searchable information for a RAG system; the exact product may also store text and other fields.
RAG can make a model's answer more relevant to selected documents, such as a company's own guides, when useful passages are retrieved.
A system can show the retrieved passages or their sources with an answer, which helps a person check where the information came from.
RAG does not guarantee a correct answer: a search may return irrelevant information, and the model may still use it badly.
In a typical RAG answer request, retrieval adds information to the model's input; retrieval by itself does not update the model's learned weights.
The original 2020 RAG research system did fine-tune its retriever and generator, so it would be inaccurate to say that every RAG system is built without training.
Some RAG designs can use search and ranking together; the search setup affects which passages reach the model.
A RAG system that searches private documents needs access controls so a user only receives information they are allowed to see.
A simple analogy is a student checking class notes before answering a question: the notes are found first, then used to form an answer.
